chief_complaint: fingers turning blue in the cold and heartburn
hpi_details: 45F presents with a history of her fingers turning stark white, then blue, then red when exposed to cold. She also complains of worsening heartburn, difficulty swallowing solid foods, and noticing the skin on her hands feels tight and shiny.
expectations: wants something for heartburn and circulation

core_concepts: Characterized by fibrosis of the skin and internal organs, and vasculopathy.
CREST syndrome: Calcinosis, Raynaud's, Esophageal dysmotility, Sclerodactyly, Telangiectasia.
common_misconceptions: Ignoring Raynaud's as a benign symptom when accompanied by systemic signs.
dangerous_errors: Giving corticosteroids to a patient with Scleroderma, which can precipitate a deadly Scleroderma Renal Crisis.
management_principles: Calcium channel blockers for Raynaud's, PPIs for GERD, monitor for interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Clinical Guidance

reference_soap.subjective: 45F with Raynaud's, severe GERD, dysphagia, and skin tightening on hands.
reference_soap.objective: Thickened, tight, shiny skin over fingers (sclerodactyly). Telangiectasias on face.
reference_soap.plan: Check anti-Centromere and anti-Scl-70 antibodies. Start PPI and Amlodipine. PFTs and Echocardiogram screening.

learning_objectives: Identify the features of CREST syndrome and the danger of corticosteroids in scleroderma.

teaching.one_liner: Raynaud's phenomenon, esophageal dysmotility, and sclerodactyly suggestive of limited systemic sclerosis (CREST).

must_ask.say: When your fingers turn cold, do they change color from white to blue to red?
Does the skin on your hands feel tight or shiny to you?
Is your heartburn worse lying down, and is it hard to swallow solid food?
Have you had any sudden severe headaches or very high blood pressure readings?
Have you noticed any shortness of breath, especially with activity?

history.answer: Whenever my hands get cold, my fingers turn completely white and then blue, and lately my heartburn has become almost unbearable.
The color changes started about two years ago, but the tight skin on my fingers and severe heartburn have gotten much worse over the past six months.
First they turn stark white and go numb, then they turn dark blue, and when I warm them up, they turn bright red and throb.
The color changes and tightness affect both of my hands and fingers, while the burning pain is right behind my breastbone.
The skin on my fingers feels stiff, thick, and shiny, almost like it is too small for my hands, making it hard to make a fist.
I have a hard time swallowing dry solid foods like bread or chicken; it feels like they get stuck behind my chest unless I drink water.
I get a severe burning feeling behind my breastbone and a sour acid taste coming up into my throat almost every night when I lie down.
Cold air, reaching into the freezer, and air-conditioned rooms bring on the attacks right away; running warm water over my hands helps bring the color back.
No, I do not have any open sores, scabs, or ulcers on my fingertips.
I have noticed a few tiny red spider-like marks on my cheeks and lips over the past year.
No, I have not had any shortness of breath or a dry cough, even when walking up stairs.
No, I have not had any severe sudden headaches, changes in my vision, or puffy swelling in my face.
My finger joints feel stiff in the mornings because the skin is so tight, but they are not red, warm, or swollen.
No, my muscles feel fine and I have not had any muscle aches or weakness in my arms or legs.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No, I have not noticed unusual dryness in my eyes or mouth.
It is getting hard to button my shirts, chop vegetables, or open jars because my fingers feel so stiff and swollen.
A clinic doctor told me two years ago that my color changes sounded like Raynaud's phenomenon, but I never had any tests done for it.
I take over-the-counter antacid tablets almost every evening, but they only give me temporary relief for an hour or two.
I have just been assuming I have poor blood circulation, which is why my hands are so sensitive to the cold.
I am really worried about why the skin on my hands is getting so tight and whether it is going to keep spreading.
I am hoping to get something stronger to relieve this heartburn and find out if there is a treatment to improve the circulation in my hands.
Other than the Raynaud's I was told about, I have never had high blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid issues, or heart trouble.
I had an uncomplicated vaginal delivery fifteen years ago, and I have never had any surgeries or hospital admissions.
I take over-the-counter antacid chewables as needed, and I do not take any prescription medications, vitamins, or herbal supplements.
I do not have any known allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes, used e-cigarettes, or used any tobacco products.
I only drink a glass of wine on rare social occasions, perhaps once or twice a month.
I work as an office administrator at an accounting firm, and I live with my husband and teenage daughter.
There is no family history of lupus, scleroderma, rheumatoid arthritis, or kidney failure; my mother had mild osteoarthritis in her knees.
My last menstrual period was two weeks ago, my periods are regular every twenty-eight days, my husband had a vasectomy, and I am definitely not pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 °C.
Well-appearing female in no acute distress, alert and conversational.
Skin over the fingers of both hands is thickened, shiny, and taut with loss of normal skin folds (sclerodactyly); scattered punctate telangiectasias noted on the cheeks and lips.
Reduced range of motion in finger flexion bilaterally due to skin tautness; no warmth, redness, or joint effusion in hands or wrists.
Radial, brachial, and dorsalis pedis pulses are normal and symmetric bilaterally with no bruits.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with normal chest excursion; no bibasilar fine crackles or wheezing.
Normal S1 and S2 with regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs, rubs, gallops, or accentuated pulmonary component (P2).
Soft, non-distended, and non-tender across all quadrants; no hepatosplenomegaly or palpable masses.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on either side.
No pitting edema in either lower extremity.
